newsitem.title: TOGO: Positions deadlocked as Zaire warring parties meet.
newsitem.headline: Positions deadlocked as Zaire warring parties meet.

text.p: Organisation of African Unity (OAU) heads of state brought Zaire's warring parties together in the same room at a special summit in Togo and allowed each to have their say, delegates said.

Wednesday's summit, convened to try to help broker a peaceful end to Zaire's civil war, provided Laurent Kabila's rebels with their first formal international platform since they began fighting to topple veteran president Mobuto Sese Seko in October.

But with the rebels having the upper hand on the battlefield and their representatives at the summit repeatedly stressing that they were not in Togo to negotiate, any more significant breakthrough looked unlikely.
"They were brought in. Both sides explained their position in front of everyone," one OAU source told Reuters.

But one senior African delegate even suggested that the fact the rebels were allowed to address Wednesday's closed session of the summit had angered the delegation from Zaire's central authorities, who listened under protest.
Ruanda had suggested that the rebel delagates be allowed to address the closed session but the delegation from Kinshasa had expected more informal contacts on the sidelines of the summit, he added.
International pressure for a ceasefire is mounting and U.N. secretary-general Kofi Annan added his voice at the meeting attended by 14 African presidents.
"I urge the parties to move to the negotiating table," said Annan, who comes from neighbouring Ghana.
"The fighting must stop and the dialogue must begin," he said.
In only five months the rebels have seized a quarter of the vast country Mobutu has ruled over like an absolute monarch since 1965.

Zaire's ragged army has collapsed in the field and the key cities of Lubumbashi and Mbuji-Mayi are in rebel sights. The two cities dominate Zaire's vast mineral wealth of copper, cobalt, diamonds and precious metals.
A rebel delegation could in future hold talks with envoys of Mobutu to prepare for a summit between Mobutu and Kabila, rebel justice commissioner Mwanze Kongolo said on Tuesday.
This drawn-out formula would allow Kabila's disciplined fighters to capture more territory, analysts noted.
Voice of the People, the rebel radio broadcasting from Goma, said both Lubumbashi and Mbuji-Mayi were "within the grip" of the rebel forces.

Expatriates in Lubumbashi with contacts nearest to the no man's land between the rebels and Zairean forces told Reuters that at the present slow advance, it would be at least 10 days before Kabila's forces reached the city.
Aid workers said Zairean troops still held at least the southern part of Lake Mweru, 300 km (180 miles) from the city.
More than 1,000 U.S., French and Belgian troops are massed in Congo, ready to evacuate Westerners from Zaire if necessary.
The rebels swiftly rejected an offer by Mobutu's party on Tuesday night to share power before elections.
"There cannot be power-sharing between us and Mobutu's people. It is impossible," their information commissioner, Raphael Nghenda, said in rebel-held Kisangani.
The offer reinforced the sense that 66-year-old Mobutu, weakened by prostate cancer, needs a truce far more than Kabila does.
Speculation that Kabila might change his mind and fly to Togo dimmed when there was no sign of him late on Wednmesday.
Back in Zaire's capital Kinshasa, where popular support for Kabila is sizeable, squabbling politicians failed to agree a candidate to take over the vacant premiership.
Aides of veteran dissident Etienne Tshisekedi said their man was unanimously picked to become prime minister, subject to Mobutu's approval, but other opposition parties denied that.

Kabila's main African sympathisers, Uganda, Rwanda, Eritrea, Ethiopia and Angola, were all absent from Togo. But Rwanda's strongman, Paul Kagame, wished the rebels every success in an interview published on Wednesday.
"It will not be very diplomatic to say this as Vice-President of a neighbouring country, but I don't like the current Zairean rulers," Kagame told Belgium's Humo.
"Why doesn't the international community understand that a number of Zaireans want to free the country of a corrupt military regime?" he asked.
